You asked to see the wording, so the AFTER picture is the wording.

First, what the arrow actually does — I read the code rather than guessing, because it decides how the message should read. Outdenting moves the item up one level and takes everything inside it along. Nothing is deleted, and the → arrow puts it back. So the dialog must not look like a danger warning — a red "are you sure?" for a reversible move trains you to click through every dialog, including the ones that matter.

What the wording does:
• asks a plain question in the title — "Move this out to its own branch?"
• names the item and its parent, so you know which row you hit
• shows the move as now → after, rather than describing it
• says what travels with it — anything inside moves too
• says it is reversible, naming the → that undoes it
• the confirm button says Move it out, not "OK" — the button names the action, so it reads correctly if you skim.

the alternative you asked about — “1st Sunday”

You said: “have it as an alternative option, and see how you want to do it, like 1st sunday of the week or something like that. see how others do it.”

I looked. Google Calendar, Outlook, ServiceNow and the iCalendar standard all do the same thing: monthly is two modes you pick between — a day number, or an nth weekday — never both at once. ServiceNow names them “Day of the month” and “Day of the week”. That is the shape in the AFTER picture: the two radio buttons at slot 2. Picking On a weekday swaps the row below for On the [first] [Sunday] of every month — first / second / third / fourth / last, by any weekday.

Why it has to be a choice, measured in your engine: the weekday boxes today are an AND, not an alternative. On a monthly rule, ticking Mo means “the 28th, but only when the 28th is a Monday” — which fires roughly once every seven months, or never. That is a trap, and it is live in your planner now.

The cause, found in the code and confirmed by driving it: the test that decides what is overdue asks only "does this item have a date in the past, and is it unticked?" It never looks at the repeat rule or at Show again. A repeating item’s stored date is its last occurrence, so every repeating routine whose last occurrence has passed is permanently overdue.

The fix, which you chose: Show again OFF → never overdue. If a missed one is meant to be skipped, it is not outstanding, so it should not be red in the tree or counted either. With the switch ON nothing changes — you chose to keep both the red row and the day-view entry, because then it genuinely is outstanding.

It still advises on every turn — that part earns its place. The gate that enforced the old way is switched off, and kept so it can be switched back.
  4. When you ask to SEE it, you get a photograph of it working — not a drawing, and not the same drawing twice. A drawing is only ever a first look at something not built yet. The moment you ask again, I build it, test it and photograph the real thing. Added 2026-10-10, after I left two drawings on this board across three replies and you had to ask three times.
  5. I do not hand anything back half done. If a card says fixed, it is built, measured, gate-tested and photographed before you read the word. Added 2026-10-10, in your words: "your response must be complete and done before saying done".
  6. I find the pattern before I invent one. Before changing how anything looks, I find the control in the planner that already does that job and copy it. Added 2026-10-10, after I drew a new calendar when the app already had one, and after I changed a css rule that three controls share instead of the one you asked about. Both came from acting on what I expected instead of measuring what is there. When you ask "is that Claude or Minimax" — it is me. Minimax writes only the exact text I dictate.
  7. Your list goes up here first. Every item you raise becomes a card with a BEFORE picture, an AFTER picture and how I would fix it. Nothing is written into the planner before that.
  8. No code before you approve the card. You approve card by card. Only when you say “make it live” do I write anything.
  9. Approved is not live. A card you approve stays here as APPROVED until the build ships, so you can see what is queued.
  10. A card never leaves until you say remove. This board is the record of what you asked for, not a list of what I finished.
  11. Your words are kept, all of them — one line per thing you said. Your first quote stays at the top of the card forever; every later correction is its own dated line underneath, never merged into a paragraph, so you can check each one off. I never replace what you said with my summary.
  12. The AFTER is not one picture — it explains the new setup, step by step, in different pictures. What happens first, what happens next, what it looks like when it works. Never the same picture twice. If nothing is built yet, the card says so in plain words instead of pretending.
  13. Every question sits inside the problem it belongs to — never collected somewhere else. You read one card and answer it there.
  14. I raise what you have not thought of. Every card carries an I also thought of note: the thing your request does not decide — the crowded case, the phone, what happens to what you already have.
  15. I test it in Safari myself — before I call it done, and again after it goes live.
  16. Pictures, not paragraphs. Short words around the picture, never an essay above it.
  17. Every picture is half a page — including the step pictures. The BEFORE and AFTER are half each, and a step picture is the same size, not a thumbnail, because you have to see what is inside it. A shot of the whole browser takes the full width on its own row.
  18. EVERY APPROVED CARD IS SHOWN CONSOLIDATED — folded shut. The moment you approve one it collapses to a single line, so the board only ever shows you what still needs you. Press open beside its number to look at it again. This one is never skipped.

How to answer: say the card number and what you want — “4 approve”, “6 I was on Week”, “14 close it”. Anything you do not mention, I leave alone. Each card has a YOUR ANSWER line at its foot showing exactly what to say. Approved cards are folded shut — press open beside the number to look at one again.
